Adenauer.context: Konrad Adenauer served as Bundeskanzler from 1949 to 1963, shaping postwar Germany.

zweite.context: In 'der Zweite Weltkrieg', the nominative form used as attributive adjective.

Weltkrieg.etymology: Welt (world) + Krieg (war), compound; first used for WWI in early 20th century
Weltkrieg.context: Refers to both World Wars, whose victims were jointly commemorated by France and Germany at Verdun.

Europa.etymology: From Greek Eurōpē, possibly from eurys (wide) + ops (eye/face).
Europa.context: Used as distractor: the Iron Curtain as Europe versus the USA.

Reichskanzler.meaning: Reich Chancellor (head of government in German Empire/Weimar)
Reichskanzler.context: Hitler was appointed Reichskanzler on 30 January 1933, beginning Nazi rule.

dritte.etymology: Old High German dritto, from drei (three); ordinal numeral
dritte.context: Drittes Reich (Third Reich) refers to the Nazi Germany period 1933-1945.

Reich.context: 'Das Dritte Reich' referred to Nazi Germany as the supposed third German empire.

Räterepublik.etymology: Compound: Räte (councils, plural of Rat) + Republik (republic, from Latin)
Räterepublik.context: Short-lived revolutionary councils republic form, as in the Bavarian Soviet Republic 1919.

Zeit.context: 'Die Zeit des Nationalsozialismus' refers to the Nazi era (1933-1945) in Germany.

Nationalsozialismus.context: The ideology of the NSDAP under Hitler; its absence of rights is a key civics topic.

willkürlich.context: Describes arrests made without legal basis, typical of totalitarian states.

Verhaftung.etymology: From 'verhaften' (to arrest), prefix ver- + 'haften' (to hold, Old High German)
Verhaftung.context: Arbitrary arrests were a key tool of Nazi oppression against political opponents.

Verfolgung.context: Refers to the systematic Nazi persecution of Jews and other minority groups.

Krieg.etymology: Middle High German 'kriec', possibly from Proto-Germanic *krīgaz
Krieg.context: The question asks which war lasted from 1939 to 1945, i.e., World War II.

dauern.etymology: Middle High German 'duren', from Latin 'durare' meaning to endure.
dauern.context: Describes the duration of the divorce process lasting one year in Germany.

Vietnamkrieg.context: Listed as a distractor answer: the Vietnam War was not the 1939-1945 conflict.

Golfkrieg.etymology: Compound: Golf (Gulf, from Arabic via Italian) + Krieg (war)
Golfkrieg.context: Listed as a distractor answer in civics tests distinguishing WWII from other wars.

kennzeichnen.context: Asks what characterized the Nazi state (NS-Staat) in terms of policies.

NS.etymology: Abbreviation of 'Nationalsozialistisch', used in compound NS-Staat
NS.context: NS-Staat refers to the National Socialist state, i.e., Nazi Germany 1933-1945.

Rassismus.context: State racism was a defining feature of NS ideology, targeting Jews and others.

Entwicklung.etymology: From 'entwickeln' (to develop), 'wickeln' (to wind) with prefix ent-
Entwicklung.context: Development of democracy was suppressed under National Socialism.

Claus.meaning: Claus (German given name, variant of Klaus/Nicholas)
Claus.etymology: Short form of Nikolaus, from Greek 'Nikolaos' (victory + people)
Claus.context: Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg was the key figure in the July 1944 assassination attempt.

Schenk.etymology: Middle High German 'schenke' (one who pours drinks), a hereditary title
Schenk.context: Part of Stauffenberg's full aristocratic name, indicating noble lineage.

Graf.etymology: Old High German 'gravo', Proto-Germanic *grabaz (one who digs/governs)
Graf.context: Graf (Count) is a German noble title in Stauffenberg's full name.

Stauffenberg.context: Claus von Stauffenberg led the 20 July 1944 assassination attempt against Hitler.

bekannt.etymology: Past participle of bekennen/kennen; Old High German kennen
bekannt.context: Used in a distractor; Stolpersteine do not specifically commemorate well-known Jewish musicians.

Goldmedaille.etymology: Compound: Gold (gold, Old High German) + Medaille (medal, from French/Italian)
Goldmedaille.context: A gold medal at the 1936 Olympics is listed as a distractor answer about Stauffenberg.

olympisch.etymology: From Greek 'Olympia', site of ancient games; Latin 'Olympicus'
olympisch.context: The 1936 Olympics were held in Berlin under the Nazi regime.

Bau.context: Construction of the Reichstag building is a distractor option in a civics question.

Reichstagsgebäude.etymology: Compound: Reichstag + Gebäude (building, from 'bauen' to build)
Reichstagsgebäude.context: The Reichstag building in Berlin is Germany's parliament; built in the 1890s.

Aufbau.etymology: From 'aufbauen' (to build up), prefix auf- + 'bauen' (to build)
Aufbau.context: Hitler's build-up of the Wehrmacht (armed forces) violated the Treaty of Versailles.

Wehrmacht.etymology: Compound: Wehr (defense) + Macht (power/force), both Old High German
Wehrmacht.context: Stauffenberg served in the Wehrmacht before organizing the assassination attempt.

Attentat.context: The Attentat on 20 July 1944 was Stauffenberg's bomb plot to kill Hitler.

Juli.etymology: From Latin 'Julius', named after Julius Caesar
Juli.context: 20 July 1944 is commemorated in Germany as the day of the resistance plot against Hitler.

zerstören.etymology: From 'stören' (to disturb) with prefix zer- (apart), Old High German
zerstören.context: Jewish shops and synagogues were destroyed by Nazis and their followers.

Synagoge.etymology: From Greek synagōgē (assembly), from syn (together) + agein (to lead).
Synagoge.context: Synagoge is the correct answer as the Jewish house of prayer.

Geschäft.context: Jewish shops were vandalized and destroyed during Kristallnacht pogrom.

passieren.context: Asks what happened on 9 November 1938, i.e., Kristallnacht in Germany.

November.etymology: From Latin 'November', originally the ninth month ('novem' = nine)
November.context: 9 November 1938 (Kristallnacht) is a key date in German Holocaust history.

Angriff.etymology: From 'angreifen' (to attack), 'greifen' (to grasp), Old High German 'grīfan'
Angriff.context: Germany's attack on Poland on 1 September 1939 marked the start of WWII.

Polen.context: The German invasion of Poland in 1939 triggered WWII and is a key civics fact.

lösen.context: The Nazis dissolved the Reichstag (parliament) to consolidate power in 1933.

Reichstag.etymology: Compound: Reich (realm) + Tag (diet/assembly day), Old High German
Reichstag.context: The Reichstag was dissolved by the Nazis after they seized power in 1933.

Anhänger.etymology: From 'anhängen' (to attach/follow), 'hängen' (to hang), Old High German
Anhänger.context: Nazi supporters participated in destroying Jewish property during Kristallnacht.

Reichspräsident.meaning: Reich President (head of state in Weimar Republic)
Reichspräsident.context: Hitler merged chancellor and president roles to become Führer after Hindenburg's death.

lassen.etymology: Old High German 'lazan', Proto-Germanic root meaning to let or leave.
lassen.context: In 'die Rechnung liegen lassen', means ignoring or leaving the invoice unaddressed.

Kurt.etymology: Short form of Konrad, Old High German 'Kuonrat' (bold counsel)
Kurt.context: Kurt Georg Kiesinger was the third Federal Chancellor of West Germany (1966-1969).

Georg.meaning: Georg (German given name, equivalent of George)
Georg.context: Middle name of Kurt Georg Kiesinger, West German Chancellor 1966-1969.

Kiesinger.etymology: German surname from place name or occupation; 'Kies' means gravel
Kiesinger.context: Kurt Georg Kiesinger served as third Bundeskanzler from 1966 to 1969.

Willy.meaning: Willy (German given name, variant of Wilhelm/William)
Willy.etymology: Short form of Wilhelm, Old High German 'Willahelm' (will + helmet)
Willy.context: Willy Brandt was the fourth West German Chancellor, known for Ostpolitik.

Brandt.etymology: German/Scandinavian surname meaning 'fire' or 'sword'; also spelled Brand
Brandt.context: Willy Brandt served as Bundeskanzler 1969-1974 and won the Nobel Peace Prize.

rufen.context: Protesters in East Germany riefen (shouted) 'Wir sind das Volk' in 1989 demonstrations.

wir.etymology: Old High German 'wir', Proto-Germanic *wīz (first person plural)
wir.context: 'Wir sind das Volk' (We are the people) was the rallying cry of the 1989 East German protests.

Arbeiteraufstand.etymology: Compound of Arbeiter (worker) + Aufstand (uprising); both from Old High German.
Arbeiteraufstand.context: Refers specifically to the June 1953 East German workers' uprising against the SED regime.

Anti.context: Used as a prefix in compound words like Anti-Atomkraft to denote opposition movements.

Atomkraft.etymology: Compound of Atom (from Greek atomos) + Kraft (power, Old High German kraft).
Atomkraft.context: Central term in West German protest movements against nuclear energy in the 1980s.

Montagsdemonstration.etymology: Compound of Montag (Monday) + Demonstration (from Latin demonstratio).
Montagsdemonstration.context: The Monday demonstrations of 1989 in the GDR were pivotal in the peaceful revolution leading to reunification.

Alliierte.etymology: From French allié, Latin alligare (to bind together).
Alliierte.context: Refers to the WWII Allied powers to whom Germany submitted.

Besatzungsmacht.etymology: Compound of Besatzung (occupation) + Macht (power); Besatzung from besetzen 'to occupy'.
Besatzungsmacht.context: The question asks which country was not an Allied Besatzungsmacht in Germany after WWII.

Sowjetunion.etymology: From Sowjet (Russian sovet 'council') + Union (Latin unio); refers to the USSR.
Sowjetunion.context: The Soviet Union was one of the four Allied occupying powers and governed the eastern zone of Germany.

Schweden.etymology: From Old Norse Svíþjóð; German form Schweden via medieval Latin Suecia.
Schweden.context: Sweden is listed as a distractor answer; it was not an Allied occupying power in Germany after WWII.

Frankreich.etymology: From the Franks (Franken) + Reich (realm); Old High German Franconorichi.
Frankreich.context: France was one of the four Allied occupying powers controlling a zone in southwestern Germany.

Italien.etymology: From Latin Italia, possibly from Oscan Víteliú 'land of cattle'.
Italien.context: Italy appears as a distractor; it was not among the Allied occupying powers in postwar Germany.

Japan.etymology: From Chinese Rìběn ('origin of the sun'); Portuguese Japão introduced to Europe.
Japan.context: Japan is listed as a distractor answer; it had no role as an occupying power in Germany after WWII.

Spanien.etymology: From Latin Hispania, possibly of Phoenician origin.
Spanien.context: Spain is listed as a distractor; it was not one of the Allied occupying powers in postwar Germany.

Portugal.etymology: From Portus Cale, a Roman settlement near modern Porto.
Portugal.context: Portugal is listed as a distractor; it was not one of the Allied occupying powers in postwar Germany.

Verbot.etymology: From verbieten 'to prohibit', from Old High German farbiotan; prefix ver- + bieten.
Verbot.context: The Verbot von Parteien (party ban) is a constitutional mechanism to protect German democracy.

Entfaltung.etymology: From entfalten 'to unfold'; prefix ent- + falten 'to fold', Old High German faldan.
Entfaltung.context: The right to freie Entfaltung der Persönlichkeit is guaranteed by Article 2 of the German Basic Law.

Persönlichkeit.etymology: From Person (Latin persona 'mask, role') + suffix -lichkeit; formed in Early Modern German.
Persönlichkeit.context: The free development of Persönlichkeit is a fundamental right under the German Basic Law.

steuern.etymology: From Old High German stiuren 'to steer'; related to Steuer (rudder).
steuern.context: Describes state control of the economy in a command economy system, contrasting with market economies.

allein.etymology: From Middle High German al ein 'all one'; Old High German einaz.
allein.context: Emphasizes that a free market economy is regulated exclusively by supply and demand without state intervention.

Angebot.etymology: From anbieten 'to offer'; prefix an- + bieten (Old High German biotan 'to offer').
Angebot.context: Angebot und Nachfrage (supply and demand) is the fundamental principle of a market economy.

Nachfrage.etymology: From nachfragen 'to inquire after'; nach (after) + fragen (Old High German frāgēn 'to ask').
Nachfrage.context: Nachfrage together with Angebot determines prices and production in a market economy.

planen.etymology: From French planer / Latin planus 'flat'; adopted into German in 18th century.
planen.context: In a planned economy (Planwirtschaft), production is geplant by the state rather than the market.

berücksichtigen.etymology: From be- + Rücksicht (consideration); Rücksicht from rück (back) + Sicht (view).
berücksichtigen.context: In a command economy, supply and demand are not berücksichtigt; the state determines production.

richten.meaning: aligns, orients (sich richten nach: to be guided by)
richten.etymology: From Old High German rihten 'to make straight'; related to recht (right, straight).
richten.context: Sich richten nach describes how export-oriented economies align production to foreign demand.

sorgen.etymology: From Old High German sorgēn 'to worry, care'; related to Sorge (worry/care).
sorgen.context: In a social market economy, the state sorgt für einen sozialen Ausgleich to balance market outcomes.

Ausgleich.etymology: From ausgleichen 'to balance out'; aus- + gleichen (Old High German gilīhhōn 'to make equal').
Ausgleich.context: The state ensures sozialer Ausgleich in Germany's social market economy to reduce inequality.

amerikanisch.etymology: From Amerika + -isch suffix; Amerika named after explorer Amerigo Vespucci
amerikanisch.context: Used as a distractor; europäische Integration does not refer to American immigrants in Europe.

französisch.etymology: From Franzose (Frenchman), derived from Franken (Franks), a Germanic tribe
französisch.context: Describes Mitterrand's nationality as French president at the Verdun commemoration.

britisch.etymology: From Latin Britannicus; referring to Britannia, from Celtic Pritanī.
britisch.context: The britische Besatzungszone covered northwestern Germany including Hamburg after World War II.

sowjetisch.context: The sowjetische Besatzungszone in eastern Germany became the GDR (DDR) in 1949.

Gründungsmitglied.etymology: Compound of Gründung (founding) + Mitglied (member); Mitglied from mit + Glied (limb).
Gründungsmitglied.context: Germany's status as a Gründungsmitglied of the EU and NATO is relevant for citizenship test knowledge.

Nordatlantikpakt.etymology: Compound of Nord (north) + Atlantik + Pakt (from Latin pactum 'agreement').
Nordatlantikpakt.context: The Nordatlantikpakt (NATO) is the collective defense alliance West Germany joined in 1955.

NATO.etymology: Acronym from English North Atlantic Treaty Organization, founded 1949.
NATO.context: Germany is a founding member of NATO, the Western military alliance formed after World War II.

vereint.etymology: Past participle of vereinen 'to unite'; from ein (one), Old High German einōn.
vereint.context: Die Vereinten Nationen (United Nations) is the international organization Germany joined in 1973.

Nation.etymology: Latin natio, from nasci (to be born)
Nation.context: Refers to the German nation as a unified political and cultural entity.

VN.etymology: German acronym for Vereinte Nationen, equivalent to English UN.
VN.context: VN is the German abbreviation for the United Nations, used alongside the English acronym UN.

europäisch.etymology: From Europa (Europe), derived from Latin Europaeus, ultimately Greek Eurōpē
europäisch.context: Inflected form (genitive plural) modifying Staaten, describing European member states.

Warschauer.etymology: Derived from Warschau (Warsaw), the Polish capital; German adjectival form.
Warschauer.context: The Warschauer Pakt was the Eastern Bloc military alliance led by the Soviet Union, opposing NATO.

Pakt.etymology: From Latin pactum, from pacisci (to agree, to covenant).
Pakt.context: The Warschauer Pakt (Warsaw Pact) was the Eastern bloc military alliance.

verteilen.etymology: From ver- + teilen 'to divide'; teilen from Old High German teilan.
verteilen.context: Refers to how Germany's occupation zones were distributed among the four Allied powers after 1945.

Sektor.etymology: From Latin sector 'cutter'; from secare 'to cut', used for divided areas.
Sektor.context: Berlin was divided into four Sektoren, each administered by one of the four Allied powers.

aufteilen.etymology: From auf- + teilen; teilen from Old High German teilan 'to divide'.
aufteilen.context: Berlin was aufgeteilt into four sectors after WWII, reflecting the four-power occupation structure.

Dresden.etymology: From Sorbian Drežďany, meaning 'people of the riverside forest'.
Dresden.context: Dresden is listed as a distractor; it was not the city divided into four sectors after WWII.

Frankfurt.etymology: From Franken (Franks) + Furt (ford/river crossing); 'Ford of the Franks'.
Frankfurt.context: Frankfurt/Oder is listed as a distractor; it was not the city divided into four sectors after WWII.

Juni.etymology: From Latin Junius (mensis), named after the Roman gens Junia or goddess Juno.
Juni.context: The Berlin Airlift began in Juni 1948 when the Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin's land routes.

West.etymology: From Old High German west, common Germanic; related to English 'west'.
West.context: West-Berlin refers to the western sectors of Berlin supplied by the Allied airlift during the blockade.

Luftbrücke.etymology: Compound of Luft (air, Old High German luft) + Brücke (bridge, Old High German brucca).
Luftbrücke.context: The Berliner Luftbrücke (1948–49) supplied West Berlin by air during the Soviet blockade.

Umstand.etymology: From umstehen 'to stand around'; um (around) + Stand (stand), Old High German umbistand.
Umstand.context: The question asks which Umstand necessitated the Berlin Airlift to supply West Berlin.

verantwortlich.etymology: From verantworten (to be accountable) + -lich; Antwort from Old High German antwurti 'answer'.
verantwortlich.context: Asks which circumstance was verantwortlich (responsible) for the need to airlift supplies to West Berlin.

Versorgung.etymology: From versorgen 'to supply'; ver- + sorgen (Old High German sorgēn 'to care').
Versorgung.context: The Versorgung of West Berlin's population by air was the purpose of the 1948–49 Berlin Airlift.

Bevölkerung.etymology: From bevölkern 'to populate'; be- + Volk (people, Old High German folk).
Bevölkerung.context: The West-Berliner Bevölkerung depended entirely on the airlift during the Soviet blockade.

Flugzeug.etymology: Compound of fliegen (to fly, Old High German fliogan) + Zeug (tool/stuff).
Flugzeug.context: Supplies were delivered to West Berlin by Flugzeug during the 1948–49 airlift.

kostengünstig.etymology: Compound of Kosten (costs, from French coûter) + günstig (favorable); comparative form.
kostengünstig.context: Listed as a (distractor) reason France preferred the airlift over land-based supply of West Berlin.

Landtransport.etymology: Compound of Land (land, Old High German lant) + Transport (from Latin transportare).
Landtransport.context: Landtransport to West Berlin was blocked by the Soviet Union, necessitating the airlift.

Angst.etymology: From Old High German angust 'distress'; Proto-Germanic *angustu-, related to Latin angustus 'narrow'.
Angst.context: Angst vor Überfällen is cited as a distractor reason for preferring the airlift over land transport.

Überfall.etymology: From überfallen 'to attack'; über (over) + fallen (Old High German fallan 'to fall').
Überfall.context: Fear of Überfällen during land transport is given as a (distractor) reason for the Berlin Airlift.

schnell.etymology: Middle High German 'snel', Old High German 'snel', meaning lively or quick.
schnell.context: Describes rapid changes in required work skills in a modern economy.

unterbrechen.etymology: From unter- + brechen (Old High German brehhan 'to break'); 'to break under/through'.
unterbrechen.context: The Soviet Union unterbrach all land traffic to West Berlin, forcing the Western Allies to use the airlift.

gesamt.etymology: From Old High German gisamt 'together'; related to zusammen and Latin simul.
gesamt.context: The Soviet Union cut off the gesamten (entire) land traffic to West Berlin during the 1948 blockade.

Verkehr.etymology: From verkehren 'to traffic'; ver- + kehren (Old High German keran 'to turn').
Verkehr.context: The Soviets blocked all Verkehr by land to West Berlin, triggering the Berlin Airlift.

Landweg.etymology: Compound of Land (land) + Weg (way, Old High German weg); 'overland path'.
Landweg.context: The Soviet blockade cut all access auf dem Landwege to West Berlin, necessitating the airlift.

enden.etymology: From Ende (end, Old High German enti) + verbal suffix -en; 'to come to an end'.
enden.context: Refers to how World War II officially endete in Europe, a key fact in the citizenship test.

offiziell.etymology: From Latin officialis (of a duty/office), via French officiel
offiziell.context: Describes January 27 as an officially recognized day of remembrance in Germany.

bedingungslos.context: Describes Germany's unconditional surrender ending WWII.

Kapitulation.etymology: From Latin capitulatio, from capitulare (to draw up terms).
Kapitulation.context: Germany's unconditional surrender is a key event in modern German history.

Rückzug.context: Refers to German military withdrawal from occupied territories after WWII.

besetzen.etymology: From be- + setzen (to set/place); Old High German sezzen
besetzen.context: An incorrect description of reunification; the DDR was not occupied but acceded to West Germany.

Revolution.etymology: From Latin revolutio, from revolvere (to roll back).
Revolution.context: The 1918 German Revolution led to the end of WWI and the Kaiser's abdication.

Ludwig.context: Ludwig Erhard was West Germany's second chancellor and architect of the Wirtschaftswunder.

Erhard.etymology: Germanic surname from Erhard, meaning strong/honorable.
Erhard.context: Ludwig Erhard championed the social market economy in postwar West Germany.

Kniefall.meaning: kneeling, act of falling to one's knees
Kniefall.context: Willy Brandt's 1970 Kniefall in Warsaw was a gesture of German contrition for WWII crimes.

Ghetto.etymology: Italian ghetto, possibly from Venetian geto (foundry), where Jews were confined.
Ghetto.context: The Warsaw Ghetto was where Brandt performed his famous act of reconciliation.

Warschau.etymology: German name for the Polish city Warszawa.
Warschau.context: Warschau is the site of Brandt's famous Kniefall and the 1970 treaty with Poland.

ausdrücken.etymology: German: aus (out) + drücken (to press), to press out meaning.
ausdrücken.context: Asked what symbolic message Brandt intended to convey through his kneeling gesture.

unterwerfen.etymology: German: unter (under) + werfen (to throw), to throw oneself under.
unterwerfen.context: Describes Germany's submission to the Allied powers after WWII.

bitten.etymology: Old High German 'bitten', Germanic root related to English 'bid'
bitten.context: Used when formally requesting permission from an authority like the Arbeitsamt.

polnisch.context: Refers to Polish Jews who were victims of German WWII persecution.

Vergebung.etymology: German: ver- + geben (to give), giving away resentment.
Vergebung.context: Brandt sought Vergebung from Poland and Polish Jews for Nazi crimes.

Demut.etymology: Old High German diomuoti, from deo (servant) + muot (spirit/mind).
Demut.context: Brandt's kneeling expressed Demut as a symbol of German acknowledgment of guilt.

Gebet.etymology: Old High German gibet, from beten (to pray), Proto-Germanic *bidōną.
Gebet.context: A prayer spoken at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is a solemn memorial act.

Grab.etymology: Old High German grab, Proto-Germanic *grabą (grave, pit).
Grab.context: Das Grab des Unbekannten Soldaten is a memorial found in many countries.

unbekannt.etymology: German: un- (not) + bekannt (known), from bekennen (to recognize).
unbekannt.context: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier honors unidentified fallen soldiers.

Gebetshaus.meaning: house of prayer, place of worship
Gebetshaus.context: Used in civic knowledge questions about Jewish places of worship.

Basilika.etymology: From Latin basilica, Greek basilikē (royal hall), from basileus (king).
Basilika.context: A basilica is a Christian church building, not a Jewish house of worship.

Moschee.etymology: From Arabic 'masjid' via Turkish 'mescit' and French 'mosquée'
Moschee.context: Mosques can legally be built in Germany as part of religious freedom guarantees.

Kirche.etymology: Old High German kirihha, from Greek kyriakon (house of the Lord)
Kirche.context: Churches in Germany are recognized institutions where citizens can also seek civic information.

Wirtschaftswunder.etymology: German: Wirtschaft (economy) + Wunder (miracle), compound noun coined in 1950s.
Wirtschaftswunder.context: Das Wirtschaftswunder describes West Germany's rapid postwar economic recovery in the 1950s.

Grundlage.context: Refers to the legal basis on which the state of Israel was founded.

Resolution.etymology: From Latin resolutio, from resolvere (to loosen, to decide).
Resolution.context: A UN Resolution provided the international legal basis for the founding of Israel.

Beschluss.etymology: German: be- + schließen (to close/decide), a concluded decision.
Beschluss.context: Refers to a formal decision by the Zionist Congress as a potential founding basis.

Zionistenkongress.etymology: German: Zionist (from Zion, Hebrew hill in Jerusalem) + Kongress (congress).
Zionistenkongress.context: The Zionistenkongress was the main governing body of the Zionist movement.

Vorschlag.etymology: German: vor (before) + schlagen (to strike/propose), a put-forward idea.
Vorschlag.context: Used as a distractor answer: a German government proposal as Israel's legal basis.

UdSSR.etymology: German abbreviation for Union der Sozialistischen Sowjetrepubliken.
UdSSR.context: A distractor answer suggesting the USSR proposed the founding of Israel.

wofür.context: Used to ask what the expression Iron Curtain stood for.

Ausdruck.etymology: German: aus (out) + Druck (pressure/print), that which is pressed out.
Ausdruck.context: Refers to the term Eiserner Vorhang as a political expression.

eisern.etymology: Old High German īsarīn, from īsarn (iron), Proto-Germanic *īsarną.
eisern.context: Part of the Cold War term Eiserner Vorhang, the Iron Curtain.

Vorhang.etymology: German: vor (before/in front) + hangen (to hang), that which hangs in front.
Vorhang.context: Eiserner Vorhang (Iron Curtain) symbolized the Cold War division between East and West.

Abschottung.etymology: German: ab- (off) + schotten (to bulkhead), nautical term for sealing off.
Abschottung.context: Describes the isolation of Warsaw Pact countries from the Western world.

Westen.etymology: Old High German westar, Proto-Germanic *westraz, direction of sunset.
Westen.context: Refers to Western democracies in the Cold War context against the Eastern bloc.

Norddeutschland.context: Used as a distractor in explaining what the Iron Curtain symbolized.

Süddeutschland.context: Used as a distractor answer in contrast to Norddeutschland.

Aufstand.etymology: German: auf (up) + Stand (stand), a rising up.
Aufstand.context: The 1953 workers' uprising in East Germany was commemorated as a West German holiday.

Feiertag.etymology: Feier (celebration) + Tag (day), from Old High German fîra and tag
Feiertag.context: Used as a distractor answer; the EU does not mandate uniform public holidays across member states.

erinnern.etymology: From er- (prefix) + inner (inner), originally 'to bring to inner mind', Middle High German
erinnern.context: Used in 'woran erinnert dieser Tag' asking what event this memorial day commemorates.

schwarz.etymology: Old High German swarz, Proto-Germanic *swartaz (black, dark).
schwarz.context: Black is the first color of the German tricolor; also part of the East German flag.

rot.context: Red is the second color of the German national flag colors.

golden.etymology: Old High German golden, from Gold (gold) + -en (suffix).
golden.context: Describes the gold stripe of the East German flag's tricolor design.

Hammer.etymology: Old High German hamar, Proto-Germanic *hamaraz (hammer, stone tool).
Hammer.context: The hammer on East Germany's flag symbolized the working class.

Zirkel.etymology: Latin circulus (circle), via Old High German zirkul.
Zirkel.context: The Zirkel on the DDR flag represented the intelligentsia.

Ährenkranz.meaning: wreath of grain ears, harvest wreath
Ährenkranz.etymology: German: Ähre (ear of grain) + Kranz (wreath), compound noun.
Ährenkranz.context: The Ährenkranz on the DDR emblem symbolized the peasantry and agricultural workers.

Preußen.etymology: From Old Prussian Prūsa, the Baltic people inhabiting the region.
Preußen.context: Preußen is offered as a distractor for which state had the DDR-style flag.

Rundfunk.etymology: German: Rund (round) + Funk (radio/spark), broadcasting in all directions.
Rundfunk.context: Rundfunk refers to public radio broadcasting in Germany.

öffnen.etymology: Old High German offanōn, from offan (open), Proto-Germanic *upanaz.
öffnen.context: The Berlin Wall was geöffnet on November 9, 1989, marking German reunification.

früh.etymology: Old High German fruo (early), comparative form früher means earlier/formerly.
früh.context: Indicates that a German state was previously part of the East German territory.

Brandenburg.etymology: Slavic Brennabor, later German Brandenburg, named after a Slavic fortress.
Brandenburg.context: Brandenburg is one of the eastern federal states that was formerly part of the DDR.

Bayern.meaning: Bavaria, a federal state in southern Germany
Bayern.etymology: Named after the Bavarii tribe; Old High German Baiovarii
Bayern.context: Bayern is the largest German federal state, relevant in civics as a distinct Bundesland.

Saarland.meaning: federal state in southwestern Germany (genitive form)
Saarland.etymology: From Saar (river name) + Land (land/region); land along the Saar river.
Saarland.context: Saarlandes is the genitive form of Saarland, used in phrases like 'Landtag des Saarlandes' referring to the state parliament.

Hessen.meaning: Hesse, a federal state in central Germany
Hessen.etymology: Named after the Chatti Germanic tribe; Latinized as Hassia
Hessen.context: Hessen is a central German Bundesland with Frankfurt as its major city.

erreichbar.etymology: From erreichen (to reach) + -bar (suffix meaning able); Middle High German reichen
erreichbar.context: Describes geographic accessibility, relevant when discussing remote German territories.

Oktober.etymology: Latin october, from octo (eight), originally the eighth month in Roman calendar
Oktober.context: 3 Oktober is German Unity Day (Tag der Deutschen Einheit), a national holiday.

feiern.meaning: to celebrate, to observe a holiday
feiern.etymology: Old High German firen, from Latin feria (holiday)
feiern.context: Used to describe how Germany observes the national holiday of reunification.

Tag.etymology: Old High German tag, Proto-Germanic dagaz
Tag.context: Tag der Deutschen Einheit (Day of German Unity) on 3 Oktober is Germany's national holiday.

Herbst.etymology: Old High German herbist, Proto-Germanic harbistaz
Herbst.context: The Herbst of 1989 refers to the peaceful revolution period leading to German reunification.

liberal.context: Contrasts liberal market economy with socialism in describing East Germany's system.

Sozialismus.etymology: From French socialisme, from Latin socialis (social)
Sozialismus.context: The DDR operated under socialism, contrasted with the West's market economy.

Sozialdemokratie.context: Describes the political transition from monarchy to social democratic governance in German history.

Thüringen.meaning: Thuringia, a federal state in central Germany
Thüringen.etymology: Named after the Thuringii Germanic tribe; Latin Thuringia
Thüringen.context: Thüringen is one of the five new eastern Bundesländer that joined Germany after reunification.

Bremen.meaning: Bremen, a city-state in northern Germany
Bremen.etymology: Old Saxon Brema, possibly from brem (edge, bank)
Bremen.context: Bremen is Germany's smallest Bundesland, consisting of two cities: Bremen and Bremerhaven.

Niedersachsen.meaning: Lower Saxony, a federal state in northern Germany
Niedersachsen.etymology: Nieder (lower) + Sachsen (Saxony), named after the Saxon tribe
Niedersachsen.context: Niedersachsen is a western Bundesland, not part of the former DDR territory.

Baden.meaning: Baden, historical region in southwest Germany
Baden.etymology: Named after Baden-Baden; from Old High German bad (bath)
Baden.context: Baden is part of the combined federal state Baden-Württemberg in southwest Germany.

Württemberg.meaning: Württemberg, historical region in southwest Germany
Württemberg.etymology: Named after Württemberg castle; possibly from personal name Wirtemberg
Württemberg.context: Württemberg combined with Baden forms Baden-Württemberg, a western German Bundesland.

Stasi.meaning: East German secret police/state security service
Stasi.etymology: Abbreviation of Staatssicherheit (state security), coined in DDR era
Stasi.context: The Stasi was the feared secret police of the DDR, monitoring citizens extensively.

Staatssicherheit.context: Ministerium für Staatssicherheit was the official name of the DDR's secret police.

Volksbildung.context: Ministerium für Volksbildung was the DDR ministry responsible for public education.

Schleswig.meaning: Schleswig, historical region in northern Germany
Schleswig.etymology: Old Norse Slesvig, from sle (estuary) + vig (bay)
Schleswig.context: Schleswig is part of Schleswig-Holstein, Germany's northernmost Bundesland.

Holstein.meaning: Holstein, historical region in northern Germany
Holstein.etymology: Medieval Latin Holsatia, from Old Saxon Holsten (forest settlers)
Holstein.context: Holstein combined with Schleswig forms the northernmost German Bundesland.

folgend.etymology: Present participle of folgen; Old High German folgēn
folgend.context: Used in quiz questions to introduce a list of options about German federal states.

Auflistung.etymology: From auflisten (to list); auf + Liste (list), from French liste
Auflistung.context: Refers to lists of Bundesländer in a civics quiz about former DDR territories.

enthalten.etymology: From ent- + halten (to hold); Old High German haltan
enthalten.context: Used in quiz format to ask which list contains only former DDR federal states.

früher.etymology: Comparative of früh (early); Old High German fruoji
früher.context: Describes the former DDR territory when discussing which Bundesländer belonged to it.

Rheinland.meaning: Rhineland, region along the Rhine river
Rheinland.context: Rheinland is part of Rheinland-Pfalz, a western German Bundesland not part of the DDR.

Pfalz.etymology: From Latin palatium (palace), referring to the imperial palace
Pfalz.context: Pfalz combined with Rheinland forms Rheinland-Pfalz, a western German Bundesland.

kalt.etymology: Old High German kalt, Proto-Germanic kaldaz
kalt.context: Part of Kalter Krieg (Cold War), the geopolitical tension between East and West blocs.

Westmacht.context: The Westmächte were the Western Allied powers; the DDR belonged to the opposing Eastern bloc.

blockfrei.meaning: non-aligned, not belonging to any bloc
blockfrei.etymology: Block (bloc) + frei (free); describes Cold War non-aligned movement
blockfrei.context: Blockfreie Staaten were nations not aligned with either NATO or Warsaw Pact during Cold War.

Wirtschaftssystem.etymology: Wirtschaft (economy) + System; Wirtschaft from Old High German wirt (host/manager)
Wirtschaftssystem.context: Asks about the DDR's economic system, which was centrally planned socialism.

Kapitalismus.etymology: From Latin caput (head/capital), via French capitalisme
Kapitalismus.context: Capitalism was the economic system of West Germany, not the DDR.

östlich.etymology: From Osten (east); Old High German ostan, Proto-Germanic austanaz
östlich.context: Refers to the five eastern Bundesländer that formerly constituted the DDR territory.

beitreten.meaning: to accede, to join, to become a member of
beitreten.etymology: From bei- + treten (to step/join); Old High German tretan
beitreten.context: The five eastern states beigetreten (acceded) to the Federal Republic, not the other way.

westlich.etymology: From Westen (west); Old High German westar, Proto-Germanic westraz
westlich.context: Used in an incorrect statement that western states joined the DDR, testing factual knowledge.

Beitritt.context: Beitritt der DDR refers to the DDR's accession to the Federal Republic of Germany in 1990.

nun.etymology: Old High German nu, Proto-Germanic nu
nun.context: Indicates that after reunification the new states now also belong to certain organizations.

auch.etymology: Old High German ouh, Proto-Germanic auk
auch.context: Indicates the new Bundesländer also became part of organizations previously only for West Germany.

OPEC.etymology: Acronym: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, founded 1960
OPEC.context: An incorrect option; Germany is not a member of OPEC after reunification.

Verteidigungsgemeinschaft.context: Europäische Verteidigungsgemeinschaft was a proposed European defense union the new states joined.

woran.meaning: at/about what, in memory of what
woran.etymology: Contraction of wo (where) + an (at/on); interrogative adverb
woran.context: Opens the question about what the Stolpersteine memorial stones commemorate.

sogenannt.etymology: From so (so) + genannt (called/named), past participle of nennen
sogenannt.context: Introduces the colloquial name Stolpersteine for the memorial brass plaques project.

Stolperstein.context: Stolpersteine are pavement plaques commemorating victims of Nazi persecution across Germany.

berühmt.etymology: From berühmen (to praise); be- + Ruhm (fame), Old High German hruom
berühmt.context: Used as a distractor answer; Stolpersteine do not commemorate famous politicians.

Opfer.etymology: Old High German opfar, from Latin operari (to work/offer)
Opfer.context: Stolpersteine commemorate Opfer des Nationalsozialismus, victims of Nazi persecution.

Verkehrstote.context: A distractor answer; Stolpersteine do not commemorate traffic accident victims.

Musiker.etymology: From Musik + -er suffix; Musik from Latin musica, Greek mousike
Musiker.context: A distractor option in the Stolpersteine question; the stones commemorate all NS victims.

Militärbündnis.etymology: Militär (military) + Bündnis (alliance); Bündnis from binden (to bind)
Militärbündnis.context: Asks which military alliance the DDR belonged to (the Warsaw Pact).

Rheinbund.meaning: Confederation of the Rhine, Napoleonic alliance
Rheinbund.context: A historical distractor; the DDR was not part of the Rheinbund, a Napoleonic-era alliance.

Europabündnis.etymology: Europa + Bündnis (alliance); a compound used as a quiz distractor
Europabündnis.context: A fictitious alliance name used as a wrong answer option in a civics quiz question.

Geheimdienst.etymology: Geheim (secret) + Dienst (service); Geheim from Old High German tougan
Geheimdienst.context: Describes the Stasi's role as the Geheimdienst (secret service) in the Third Reich context.

Gedenkstätte.etymology: Gedenken (to commemorate) + Stätte (place); from Old High German steti
Gedenkstätte.context: A Gedenkstätte is a memorial site honoring historical events or victims, common in Germany.

ereignen.meaning: to occur, to take place, to happen
ereignen.etymology: From er- + Auge (eye), originally 'to bring before the eyes'; Middle High German erougen
ereignen.context: Introduces the question about the workers' uprising of 17 June 1953 in the DDR.

feierlich.etymology: From Feier (celebration) + -lich suffix, Middle High German vîerlich
feierlich.context: Used to describe the formal, ceremonious nature of East Germany's accession to the Warsaw Pact.

landesweit.etymology: Compound of Land (country) + weit (wide), common German compound pattern
landesweit.context: Describes strikes that spread across the entire country, as in the 1953 East German uprising.

Streik.etymology: Borrowed from English 'strike' in 19th century labor movement context
Streik.context: Refers to nationwide labor strikes, a key element of political unrest in the GDR era.

Volksaufstand.etymology: Compound of Volk (people) + Aufstand (uprising/revolt), Germanic roots
Volksaufstand.context: Refers to the June 1953 East German popular uprising against the SED regime.

SED.meaning: Socialist Unity Party of East Germany
SED.etymology: Abbreviation of Sozialistische Einheitspartei Deutschlands, founded 1946
SED.context: The ruling communist party of the GDR, whose first party congress marked a key political milestone.

Parteitag.etymology: Compound of Partei (party) + Tag (day/congress), standard German political term
Parteitag.context: The SED-Parteitag was the governing congress of East Germany's ruling party.

Besuch.etymology: From besuchen (to visit), Middle High German besuochen, suchen (to seek)
Besuch.context: Refers to Fidel Castro's first official state visit to East Germany, a significant Cold War event.

Fidel.meaning: Fidel (given name, referring to Fidel Castro)
Fidel.context: Refers to Cuban leader Fidel Castro in the context of his visit to the GDR.

Castro.meaning: Castro (genitive form of the surname Castro)
Castro.context: Genitive form indicating the visit belonged to Fidel Castro, Cuban revolutionary leader.

Ostvertrag.meaning: Eastern Treaties (West Germany's treaties with Eastern bloc)
Ostvertrag.etymology: Compound of Ost (east) + Vertrag (treaty), plural Verträge; key term of Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik
Ostvertrag.context: The Ostverträge were treaties normalizing relations with Eastern Europe, associated with Chancellor Brandt.

Kohl.etymology: German surname from Kohl (cabbage), common family name
Kohl.context: Helmut Kohl was the German Chancellor who led German reunification in 1990.

Michail.etymology: Russian form of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el (who is like God)
Michail.context: First name of Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, key figure in the end of the Cold War.

Gorbatschow.etymology: German transliteration of Russian Горбачёв, from gorbaty (hunchbacked)
Gorbatschow.context: Mikhail Gorbachev was the Soviet leader whose reforms contributed to German reunification.

voll.etymology: Old High German fol, related to English 'full', Proto-Germanic *fullaz
voll.context: Used in the phrase 'mit vollem Namen' meaning 'by its full/official name'.

Name.etymology: Old High German namo, Proto-Germanic *namô, related to Latin nomen
Name.context: Refers to Germany's official full name, Bundesrepublik Deutschland.

Bundesbezirk.etymology: Compound of Bundes- (federal) + Bezirk (district), from French district
Bundesbezirk.context: A distractor answer in citizenship tests; Germany is not called Bundesbezirk but Bundesrepublik.

Million.etymology: From Italian milione, augmentative of mille (thousand), via French million
Million.context: Used to express Germany's population in approximate figures in civic education contexts.

Farbe.etymology: Old High German farawa, Proto-Germanic *farwō, related to fair/appearance
Farbe.context: Refers to the colors of the German national flag: black, red, and gold.

gold.etymology: Old High German gold, Proto-Germanic *gulþą, related to English 'gold'
gold.context: The third color of the German flag; schwarz-rot-gold are the official national colors.

grün.etymology: Old High German gruoni, Proto-Germanic *grōniz, related to English 'green'
grün.context: Used as a distractor in flag color questions; green is not a color of the German national flag.

gelb.etymology: Old High German gelo, Proto-Germanic *gelwaz, related to English 'yellow'
gelb.context: Appears as a distractor answer; yellow is sometimes confused with gold in the German flag.

Plenarsaal.etymology: Compound of plenar- (Latin plenus, full) + Saal (hall); term for parliament's main chamber
Plenarsaal.context: The Plenarsaal of the Bundestag is where the federal eagle symbol is prominently displayed.

sehen.etymology: Old High German sehan, Proto-Germanic *sehwaną, related to English 'see'
sehen.context: Used in the infinitive construction 'zu sehen' meaning 'to be seen/visible' in the Bundestag chamber.

Fahne.etymology: Old High German fano, Proto-Germanic *fanô, related to Latin pannus (cloth)
Fahne.context: Refers to the flag of the city of Berlin, a distractor answer for the Bundestag symbol question.

Reichsadler.etymology: Compound of Reich (empire) + Adler (eagle); symbol of the Holy Roman and German empires
Reichsadler.context: The Reichsadler is a historical imperial symbol; the modern Bundestag displays the Bundesadler.

Reichskrone.meaning: imperial crown (of the Holy Roman Empire)
Reichskrone.etymology: Compound of Reich (empire) + Krone (crown), from Latin corona
Reichskrone.context: A distractor answer; the Reichskrone is a historical artifact, not displayed in the Bundestag.

Zeitraum.etymology: Compound of Zeit (time) + Raum (space/room), reflecting German conceptualization of time as space
Zeitraum.context: Used to ask about the historical period during which the GDR existed (1949–1990).

Wiedervereinigung.etymology: Compound of wieder (again) + Vereinigung (unification), from vereinigen (to unite)
Wiedervereinigung.context: Refers to German reunification in 1990 when East Germany joined the Federal Republic.

hinzu.meaning: in addition, added to (separable prefix particle)
hinzu.etymology: Combination of hin (thither) + zu (to), directional/additive particle in German
hinzu.context: Part of the verb 'hinzukommen' (to be added), describing new states added to Germany in 1990.

Grenze.etymology: From Slavic granica (border), borrowed into German in the medieval period
Grenze.context: Refers to Germany's current borders, established at a specific point after reunification.

Januar.etymology: From Latin Ianuarius, named after the god Janus (god of beginnings and gates)
Januar.context: January 27 is Germany's official Holocaust Remembrance Day, commemorating Auschwitz liberation.

Gedenktag.etymology: Compound of Gedenk- (gedenken, to remember/commemorate) + Tag (day)
Gedenktag.context: January 27 is Germany's Gedenktag for victims of National Socialism, especially the Holocaust.

Verabschiedung.meaning: adoption, passing (of a law or document)
Verabschiedung.etymology: From verabschieden (to dismiss/adopt), derived from Abschied (farewell/departure)
Verabschiedung.context: A distractor answer; the Verabschiedung des Grundgesetzes is not what January 27 commemorates.

Befreiung.etymology: From befreien (to liberate), from frei (free), Old High German frī
Befreiung.context: January 27 commemorates the liberation of Auschwitz concentration camp in 1945.

Vernichtungslager.etymology: Compound of Vernichtung (annihilation) + Lager (camp); Vernichtung from vernichten (to annihilate)
Vernichtungslager.context: Auschwitz was the largest Nazi Vernichtungslager; its liberation is commemorated on January 27.

Auschwitz.meaning: Auschwitz (Nazi extermination camp in occupied Poland)
Auschwitz.etymology: German name for Polish town Oświęcim; site of the largest Nazi concentration and death camp
Auschwitz.context: Auschwitz was liberated on January 27, 1945, which is why this date is Germany's Holocaust memorial day.

Schengener.meaning: of Schengen (relating to the Schengen Agreement)
Schengener.etymology: Derived from Schengen, a town in Luxembourg where the 1985 treaty was signed
Schengener.context: Schengener Abkommen refers to the treaty creating Europe's passport-free travel zone.

Abkommen.etymology: From abkommen (to come to an agreement), compound of ab- + kommen (to come)
Abkommen.context: The Schengener Abkommen established free movement across participating European countries.

Passkontrolle.etymology: Compound of Pass (passport) + Kontrolle (control/check), from French contrôle
Passkontrolle.context: Within the Schengen Area, Germans can travel to many European countries without Passkontrolle.

reisen.etymology: Middle High German reisen (to travel/set out), Old High German reisan
reisen.context: Germans can reisen to many Schengen countries without passport checks under the Schengen Agreement.

Personenkontrolle.meaning: personal identity check, border control of persons
Personenkontrolle.etymology: Compound of Person (person) + Kontrolle (control/check), from Latin persona + French contrôle
Personenkontrolle.context: A distractor claim; not all people can enter Germany without Personenkontrolle under Schengen rules.

einreisen.etymology: Compound of ein- (in/into) + reisen (to travel); separable verb for cross-border entry
einreisen.context: Used in the context of border crossing rules under the Schengen Agreement.

Euro.etymology: Named after Europe (Europa), adopted as the EU's common currency name in 1995
Euro.context: A distractor answer; not every Schengen country uses the Euro as its currency.

Nachbarland.etymology: Compound of Nachbar (neighbor) + Land (country); Nachbar from Old High German nāhgibūr
Nachbarland.context: Questions about Germany's Nachbarländer test knowledge of which countries share a border with Germany.

Ungarn.etymology: German name for Hungary; derived from medieval Latin Hungaria, from the Huns or Onogurs
Ungarn.context: Ungarn is a distractor answer; it does not share a border with Germany.

Schweiz.etymology: From the canton of Schwyz, itself possibly from Old High German swedan (to burn/clear land)
Schweiz.context: Die Schweiz shares a southern border with Germany and is one of its nine neighboring countries.

Rumänien.etymology: German name for Romania; derived from Latin Romani (Romans), reflecting Roman heritage
Rumänien.context: Rumänien is a distractor answer; it does not share a border with Germany.

Bulgarien.etymology: German name for Bulgaria; from the Bulgars, a Turkic people who settled the region
Bulgarien.context: Bulgarien is a distractor answer; it does not share a border with Germany.

Griechenland.etymology: From Griech- (Greek), derived via Latin Graecia from the tribal name Graeci
Griechenland.context: Griechenland is a distractor answer; it does not border Germany.

einheitlich.etymology: From Einheit (unity) + -lich suffix; Einheit from ein (one) + -heit (abstract suffix)
einheitlich.context: Used as a distractor phrase; the EU is not formally called 'Einheitliche Union'.

deutschsprachig.etymology: Compound of deutsch (German) + sprachig (from Sprache, language), describing language communities
deutschsprachig.context: Austria has a large deutschsprachige Bevölkerung and is the most prominent German-speaking neighbor.

Tschechien.etymology: German name from Tscheche (Czech person), from the Slavic tribal name Čech
Tschechien.context: Tschechien is a distractor answer for the German-speaking population question; Czech is spoken there.

Norwegen.etymology: German name for Norway; from Old Norse Norvegr (northern way/path)
Norwegen.context: Norwegen is a distractor answer; it has no significant German-speaking population.

Österreich.etymology: Old High German Ostarrîchi (eastern realm), recorded 996 CE; referencing its eastern location
Österreich.context: Österreich is the correct answer; it has the largest German-speaking population outside Germany.

Finnland.etymology: German name for Finland; from Finns, a people name of uncertain etymology
Finnland.context: Finnland is a distractor answer; Finnish, not German, is the dominant language there.

Dänemark.etymology: From Dänen (Danes) + Mark (border territory); Danish: Danmark, meaning land of the Danes
Dänemark.context: Dänemark borders Germany to the north but has no major German-speaking population.

Osterweiterung.etymology: Compound of Ost (east) + Erweiterung (expansion), from erweitern (to expand/widen)
Osterweiterung.context: NATO-Osterweiterung refers to NATO's eastward expansion; a distractor for the reunification question.

Gemeinschaft.etymology: From gemein (common) + -schaft (abstract suffix); Old High German gimeini
Gemeinschaft.context: Europäische Gemeinschaft was an earlier name for the EU; a distractor in questions about reunification.

Luxemburg.etymology: From Old High German Lucilinburhuc (little fortress), name of the founding castle
Luxemburg.context: Luxemburg is both a neighbor of Germany and the location where the Schengen Agreement was signed.

nämlich.etymology: Middle High German nämlich, from name (name) + -lich, meaning 'by name' or 'specifically'
nämlich.context: Used to introduce a clarification or specification, here specifying the election interval.

Integration.context: Europäische Integration refers to the process of European countries uniting politically and economically.

Einwanderin.context: Used in gender-inclusive language alongside Einwanderer to refer to female immigrants.

Einwanderer.etymology: From einwandern (to immigrate), from ein- (in) + wandern (to wander/migrate)
Einwanderer.context: Refers to people who move into a country, key term in German immigration discourse.

Einwanderungsstopp.context: Refers to a policy halting immigration into a country or region like Europe.

Auswanderin.context: Female form of emigrants, used in gender-inclusive reference to European women emigrating to the USA.

Auswanderer.etymology: From auswandern (to emigrate), aus- (out) + wandern (to wander/travel)
Auswanderer.context: Refers to Europeans who left their home country to settle in the USA.

Zusammenschluss.context: Describes the political and economic unification of European states into the EU.

Kommission.etymology: From Latin commissio (entrustment), via French commission
Kommission.context: The European Commission is the executive branch of the EU, proposing legislation and enforcing treaties.

eintreten.etymology: ein- (in) + treten (to step), Old High German tretan
eintreten.context: Refers to countries being permitted to join/enter the EU as member states.

London.etymology: From Latin Londinium, possibly pre-Celtic origin
London.context: Listed as a wrong-answer option; London is not a seat of the European Parliament.

Paris.etymology: From Latin Lutetia Parisiorum, named after the Gaulish Parisii tribe
Paris.context: Listed as a distractor; Paris is not a seat of the European Parliament.

Straßburg.etymology: From Old High German Straßburg, 'city on the road/street'; French: Strasbourg
Straßburg.context: One of the official seats of the European Parliament, located in northeastern France.

damalig.etymology: From damals (at that time) + adjectival suffix -ig
damalig.context: Used to describe Mitterrand and Kohl as the leaders they were at the time of the Verdun ceremony.

Staatspräsident.context: Refers to François Mitterrand in his role as the French head of state.

François.etymology: French form of Franciscus, meaning 'Frenchman' or 'free man', from Latin Franciscus
François.context: The first name of French President Mitterrand, mentioned in the context of the Verdun commemoration.

Mitterrand.etymology: French surname, likely from a place name; François Mitterrand was French president 1981–1995
Mitterrand.context: French president who stood with Helmut Kohl at Verdun, symbolizing Franco-German reconciliation.

gedenken.etymology: ge- (prefix) + denken (to think), Old High German denken; denotes solemn remembrance
gedenken.context: Describes the act of commemorating the war dead jointly at Verdun, a symbol of European reconciliation.

Verdun.meaning: Verdun (city in France, WWI battle site)
Verdun.etymology: From Latin Verodunum, a Gaulish place name; site of one of WWI's bloodiest battles
Verdun.context: The 1984 Verdun ceremony where Kohl and Mitterrand held hands became an iconic symbol of reconciliation.

gemeinsam.etymology: From gemein (common) + -sam (suffix), Old High German gimeini
gemeinsam.context: Emphasizes the joint nature of the commemoration, symbolizing unity between former enemies.

Tote.etymology: From tot (dead), Old High German tod; nominalized adjective meaning 'dead persons'
Tote.context: Refers to the soldiers of both World Wars who died, honored at the Verdun commemoration.

Treffen.etymology: Nominalized infinitive of treffen (to meet), Old High German treffan
Treffen.context: The Verdun meeting between Kohl and Mitterrand exemplified the EU goal of lasting peace and friendship.

deutlich.etymology: From Deutung (interpretation), related to deuten (to point/interpret), Old High German diuten
deutlich.context: Used predicatively: the EU goal of reconciliation becomes evident/clear at this historic meeting.

Freundschaft.etymology: Freund (friend) + -schaft (suffix denoting state/condition), Old High German friuntscaf
Freundschaft.context: Used as a core EU goal; friendship between nations replaces historical enmity.

zwischen.etymology: Old High German zwisken, from zwei (two) + locative suffix; meaning 'in the middle of two'
zwischen.context: Preposition expressing the bilateral relationship of friendship between England and Germany.

England.etymology: From Old English Englaland, 'land of the Angles', a Germanic tribe
England.context: Used here as a distractor example; England/UK left the EU via Brexit in 2020.

Reisefreiheit.etymology: Reise (journey/travel) + Freiheit (freedom); compound noun expressing liberty to travel
Reisefreiheit.context: A key EU benefit: citizens can travel freely across all EU member states without border controls.

Frieden.etymology: Old High German fridu, from Germanic *friþuz; related to 'free' and 'friendship'
Frieden.context: Peace is stated as a central goal of the EU, especially given Europe's history of wars.

Mitgliedstaat.etymology: Mitglied (member) + Staat (state); Mitglied from mit (with) + Glied (limb/link)
Mitgliedstaat.context: Refers to the countries that are full members of the EU, currently 27 member states.

Inhalt.etymology: From inhalten (to contain), in- + halten (to hold), Old High German haltan
Inhalt.context: Asks about what the Treaties of Rome contained — their substance and provisions.

römisch.etymology: From Rom (Rome), Latin Romanus; adjective meaning 'of or from Rome'
römisch.context: Inflected form describing the Treaties of Rome (1957), which founded the EEC.

Vertrag.etymology: From vertragen (to bear/carry away), ver- + tragen (to carry); evolved to mean 'agreement'
Vertrag.context: The Treaties of Rome (1957) were foundational agreements establishing the European Economic Community.

Gründung.etymology: From gründen (to found), from Grund (ground/foundation), Old High German grunt
Gründung.context: Refers to the establishment of the European Economic Community through the Treaties of Rome in 1957.

Wirtschaftsgemeinschaft.etymology: Wirtschaft (economy) + Gemeinschaft (community); compound of Wirtschaft (from Wirt, host/manager)
Wirtschaftsgemeinschaft.context: The EWG (European Economic Community) was founded in 1957 and later evolved into the EU.

EWG.etymology: Abbreviation of Europäische Wirtschaftsgemeinschaft; predecessor organization to the EU
EWG.context: The EWG was established by the Treaties of Rome in 1957 as the precursor to the European Union.

Verpflichtung.etymology: From verpflichten (to obligate), ver- + Pflicht (duty), Old High German pfliht
Verpflichtung.context: Used as a distractor option; Germany's obligation to pay war reparations was not part of the Treaties of Rome.

Reparationsleistung.etymology: Reparation (from Latin reparare, to repair) + Leistung (performance/payment); compound noun
Reparationsleistung.context: War reparations were a post-WWI obligation for Germany, not related to the 1957 Treaties of Rome.

Festlegung.etymology: From festlegen (to fix/determine), fest (firm) + legen (to lay), Old High German festi
Festlegung.context: Used as a distractor; the Oder-Neisse line was fixed by post-WWII agreements, not the Treaties of Rome.

Neiße.etymology: Slavic origin; the river name Nysa/Neiße; defines part of the German-Polish border
Neiße.context: The Oder-Neiße line established the eastern border of Germany after WWII, confirmed by later treaties.

Linie.etymology: From Latin linea (thread, line), via Middle High German linie
Linie.context: Refers to the Oder-Neisse Line, the border between Germany and Poland established after WWII.

Ostgrenze.etymology: Ost (east, Old High German ōst) + Grenze (border, from Slavic granica)
Ostgrenze.context: The Oder-Neiße Line serves as Germany's eastern border with Poland, confirmed by treaty in 1990.

Ort.etymology: Old High German ort, meaning 'point, edge, place'; related to English 'art' in place names
Ort.context: Asks about the places where the European Parliament conducts its work (Strasbourg, Brussels, Luxembourg).

Haag.etymology: Dutch 's-Gravenhage; Haag from 'hedge/enclosure', referring to the royal hunting grounds
Haag.context: The Hague is seat of international courts but not a working location of the European Parliament.

Brüssel.etymology: From Old Dutch Bruocsella, 'settlement in the marsh'; French: Bruxelles
Brüssel.context: Brussels is one of the main seats of the European Parliament and home to major EU institutions.

Rom.etymology: From Latin Roma; possibly from Etruscan Ruma or related to Tiber River's ancient name
Rom.context: Rome gave its name to the 1957 Treaties of Rome but is not a working seat of the European Parliament.

Bern.etymology: Possibly from Bär (bear) in local legend; founded 1191 by Duke Berchtold V of Zähringen
Bern.context: Bern is the Swiss capital; Switzerland is not an EU member, so not a European Parliament location.

Wien.etymology: From Latin Vindobona, a Celtic-Roman settlement; possibly from Celtic vindo (white) + bona (base)
Wien.context: Vienna is Austria's capital; it is not a seat of the European Parliament.

Zürich.etymology: From Latin Turicum, possibly from Celtic; Switzerland's largest city and financial center
Zürich.context: Zurich is a major Swiss city; Switzerland is not an EU member, so it is not a Parliament location.

Mailand.etymology: German name for Milano; from Latin Mediolanum, 'middle of the plain'
Mailand.context: Milan is an Italian city but not a working seat of the European Parliament.

Hamburger.etymology: Derived from Hamburg (city), from Hammaburg (Old Saxon); -er suffix forms city adjectives
Hamburger.context: Used as a distractor option for naming the Treaties; 'Hamburger Verträge' is not a real EU treaty.

Pariser.etymology: From Paris + -er suffix, forming an indeclinable adjective from a city name
Pariser.context: Distractor option; 'Pariser Verträge' (1954) existed but are not the same as the Treaties of Rome.

Londoner.etymology: From London + -er suffix, forming an indeclinable adjective from the city name
Londoner.context: Used as a distractor; the 'Londoner Verträge' are not the foundational EU treaties.

bar.etymology: From Middle High German bar, meaning 'ready money'; related to 'bare' as in immediate payment
bar.context: Refers to paying with euro banknotes and coins in cash, as opposed to card or electronic payment.

Seger.etymology: German surname derived from the given name Seger/Sieger (victor), from Old High German sigu (victory)
Seger.context: Frau Seger is used as a fictional character in a civic exam question about applying for parental allowance.

tun.etymology: Old High German tuon, Proto-Germanic *dōną; cognate with English 'do'
tun.context: Used in the question asking what action Frau Seger must take to receive Elterngeld (parental allowance).

Elterngeld.etymology: Eltern (parents) + Geld (money); state benefit paid to parents after a child's birth
Elterngeld.context: Elterngeld is a German state benefit supporting parents who reduce work after having a child.

Krankenkasse.meaning: health insurance fund, statutory health insurer
Krankenkasse.etymology: Krank (sick) + Kasse (cash box/fund); Kasse from Latin capsa (box)
Krankenkasse.context: Distractor answer; Elterngeld is not applied for through the Krankenkasse but through the Elterngeldstelle.

Antrag.etymology: From antragen (to apply/propose), an- + tragen (to carry); evolved to mean formal application
Antrag.context: To receive Elterngeld, parents must submit a formal Antrag (application) to the responsible office.

Elterngeldstelle.etymology: Elterngeld (parental allowance) + Stelle (office/place); compound denoting the responsible authority
Elterngeldstelle.context: The Elterngeldstelle is the official agency where parents must submit their application for parental allowance.

stellen.etymology: Old High German stellen, from Proto-Germanic *stallijaną; to place or set something
stellen.context: In the phrase 'einen Antrag stellen', stellen means to submit or file a formal application.

nichts.etymology: From Middle High German nihtes, genitive of niht (not); literally 'of nothing'
nichts.context: Used in a distractor answer suggesting no action is needed; in reality, Elterngeld requires an application.

Arbeitsamt.etymology: Arbeit (work) + Amt (office); traditional name for the public employment agency
Arbeitsamt.context: Distractor answer; the Arbeitsamt handles unemployment, not Elterngeld applications.

Erlaubnis.etymology: From erlauben (to allow/permit), er- + lauben, Old High German irlouben (to grant leave)
Erlaubnis.context: Distractor: parents do not need permission from the Arbeitsamt to receive Elterngeld.

Kindergarten.etymology: German compound: Kinder (children) + Garten (garden), coined by Friedrich Froebel 1840
Kindergarten.context: In Germany, attendance at Kindergarten is decided by the parents or legal guardians.

Erziehungsberechtigte.meaning: legal guardians, persons with parental authority
Erziehungsberechtigte.context: Refers to parents or legal guardians who have authority over a child's education and welfare.

Maik.meaning: male given name (German variant of Mike)
Maik.etymology: German spelling variant of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el meaning 'who is like God'
Maik.context: Used as a sample name in civics questions about demonstration rights in Germany.

Sybille.meaning: female given name (German form of Sybil)
Sybille.etymology: From Latin Sibylla, from Greek Sibylla meaning prophetess or oracle
Sybille.context: Used as a sample name in civics questions about rights to hold demonstrations.

Freund.etymology: Old High German 'friunt', Proto-Germanic *frijōndz (one who loves)
Freund.context: Two friends being denied entry to a public pool due to skin color illustrates discrimination in Germany.

abhalten.etymology: German separable verb: ab (off/away) + halten (to hold), Old High German 'haltan'
abhalten.context: Used to describe the act of organizing and conducting a public demonstration on a street.

vorher.etymology: German compound: vor (before) + her (from/here), denoting prior timing
vorher.context: Refers to steps that must be completed before holding a demonstration in Germany.

anmelden.meaning: to register, to notify authorities officially
anmelden.etymology: German separable verb: an (at) + melden (to report), Middle High German 'melden'
anmelden.context: In Germany, demonstrations must be officially registered with local authorities beforehand.

jederzeit.etymology: German compound: jeder (every) + Zeit (time), Middle High German origin
jederzeit.context: Used to emphasize that demonstrations are permitted at any time everywhere in Germany.

überall.etymology: Old High German 'ubarall', compound of über (over/above) + all (all)
überall.context: Indicates that demonstrations may theoretically take place anywhere in Germany.

grundsätzlich.context: Here used ironically in a false answer claiming demonstrations are generally prohibited in Germany.

brauchen.etymology: Old High German 'bruhhan', meaning to use or make use of
brauchen.context: Used to ask what school qualification is needed to begin university studies in Germany.

Studium.etymology: From Latin studium (zeal, study), from studere (to be eager)
Studium.context: Refers to the formal program of academic study pursued at a German university.

Abitur.meaning: German university entrance qualification, A-levels equivalent
Abitur.etymology: From Latin abiturus (about to leave), from abire (to go away/depart)
Abitur.context: The Abitur is the standard school-leaving qualification required for university admission in Germany.

Diplom.etymology: From Greek diploma (folded document), from diploun (to double)
Diplom.context: A Diplom is a degree awarded after completing university studies, not an entry requirement.

Prokura.meaning: commercial power of attorney, authorized signatory status
Prokura.etymology: From Italian procura (proxy), from Latin procurare (to take care of)
Prokura.context: Prokura is a business/legal term for authorized signatory power, not an academic qualification.

Gesellenprüfung.meaning: journeyman's examination, trade apprenticeship final exam
Gesellenprüfung.context: The Gesellenprüfung concludes a vocational apprenticeship, not a prerequisite for university.

Paar.etymology: From Latin par (equal), entering German via Old French
Paar.context: Refers to two people in a romantic relationship who wish to live together in Germany.

zusammenleben.etymology: German compound: zusammen (together) + leben (to live), Old High German 'lebên'
zusammenleben.context: The question asks which couple is legally prohibited from cohabiting in Germany.

Hans.meaning: male given name (German form of John)
Hans.etymology: German short form of Johannes, from Hebrew Yohanan meaning 'God is gracious'
Hans.context: Used as a sample name in a civics question about cohabitation rights in Germany.

Marie.meaning: female given name (German/French form of Mary)
Marie.etymology: From Latin Maria, from Hebrew Miriam; meaning uncertain, possibly 'beloved'
Marie.context: Used as a sample name in a civics question about who may legally live together in Germany.

Tom.meaning: male given name (short form of Thomas)
Tom.etymology: Short form of Thomas, from Aramaic meaning 'twin'
Tom.context: Sample name used to illustrate a same-sex couple in a question about cohabitation in Germany.

Klaus.meaning: male given name (German short form of Nicholas)
Klaus.etymology: German short form of Nikolaus, from Greek Nikolaos meaning 'victory of the people'
Klaus.context: Sample name used alongside Tom in a civics question about legal cohabitation in Germany.

Sofie.context: Sample name used in a civics question about which couples may legally live together in Germany.

Lisa.meaning: female given name (short form of Elisabeth)
Lisa.etymology: Short form of Elisabeth, from Hebrew Elisheba meaning 'my God is abundance'
Lisa.context: Sample name used alongside Sofie in a question about cohabitation rights in Germany.

Anne.etymology: From Hebrew Hannah meaning 'grace' or 'favor', via Latin Anna
Anne.context: Used as a minor-aged sample person in a question about who may not legally cohabit in Germany.

Tim.meaning: male given name (short form of Timothy)
Tim.etymology: Short form of Timotheus, from Greek meaning 'honoring God'
Tim.context: Used as an adult sample person paired with a minor in a question about legal cohabitation.

volljährig.etymology: German compound: voll (full) + jährig (year-old); meaning having completed full years of majority
volljährig.context: Describes the daughter as a legal adult whose personal decisions parents cannot override.

schwanger.etymology: Old High German 'swangar', related to Old English 'swongor' meaning heavy/sluggish
schwanger.context: Describes the condition of a woman who is afforded special legal protections in Germany before and after childbirth.

kurz.etymology: Old High German 'kurz', from Latin curtus meaning short or cut
kurz.context: Used adverbially to mean 'shortly before and after' childbirth when describing legal protections.
